chapter.title: Carbohydrate Metabolism I: Glycolysis, Glycogen, Gluconeogenesis, and the Pentose Phosphate Pathway
chapter.scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: GLUT transporters mediate facilitated diffusion of glucose. Transport direction depends on the gradient and cellular context rather than an intrinsic one-way pump.
SGLT carriers couple glucose entry to sodium movement, using the sodium electrochemical gradient. The sodium–potassium ATPase helps maintain that driving gradient.
Insulin promotes GLUT4 recruitment to the surface of skeletal muscle and adipose cells. Many other glucose transporters are not acutely recruited in this way.
Glucose phosphorylation lowers free intracellular glucose and supports continued uptake. Transport and intracellular trapping are different steps.

steps.text: Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvates in the cytosol. Two ATP are invested and four are produced, giving a net of two ATP plus two NADH per glucose.
Hexokinase or glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase catalyze strongly regulated steps. PFK-1 commits carbon to glycolysis under typical cellular conditions.
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue when respiratory reoxidation of cytosolic NADH is limited. Lactate formation adds no ATP directly.
Oxygen is not a direct glycolytic substrate. Glycolysis can occur in cells lacking mitochondria, including mature human red blood cells.

steps.text: Dietary fructose and galactose can feed central carbohydrate metabolism after specific enzyme steps. They do not all enter through the same initial reaction.
In liver, fructokinase and aldolase B route fructose carbon toward triose intermediates, bypassing the PFK-1 entry step. This does not abolish every form of metabolic regulation.
Galactose is converted through the Leloir pathway toward glucose-derived intermediates. Blocking a pathway enzyme can accumulate upstream compounds.

steps.text: The mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA with CO2 release and NAD+ reduction. The reaction links glycolysis to acetyl-unit oxidation.
Its cofactors include TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD and NAD+. These helpers support decarboxylation, acyl transfer and electron transfer in the complex.
Phosphorylation by PDH kinase inhibits PDH in the standard mammalian model; dephosphorylation activates it. Energy-rich signals tend to restrain pyruvate oxidation.
PDH is effectively irreversible in human metabolism. Acetyl-CoA cannot simply reverse PDH to supply net pyruvate for glucose synthesis.

steps.text: Glycogenesis extends glycogen using activated glucose donors. Glycogen synthase makes alpha(1→4) linkages and branching enzyme introduces alpha(1→6) branches.
Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate from nonreducing ends. A debranching enzyme handles branch regions that phosphorylase cannot fully resolve.
Liver glycogen supports blood glucose because liver can release free glucose. Skeletal muscle generally uses its glycogen locally and lacks appreciable glucose-6-phosphatase activity.
Insulin favors glycogen storage, while glucagon stimulates hepatic mobilization. Epinephrine can promote mobilization in muscle; glucagon does not directly play the same muscle role.

steps.text: Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from precursors such as lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids. It is not a simple reversal of every glycolytic enzyme step.
Pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase bypass pyruvate kinase through oxaloacetate. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase bypass other strongly favorable glycolytic steps.
Synthesis of one glucose from two pyruvates uses four ATP, two GTP and two NADH. Carbon source changes can alter the accounting required.
Humans cannot obtain net glucose carbon from even-chain fatty-acid acetyl-CoA. Glycerol from triacylglycerol and propionyl-CoA from odd chains are different cases.

steps.text: The pentose phosphate pathway branches from glucose-6-phosphate. Its oxidative phase generates NADPH and releases CO2; its nonoxidative phase rearranges sugar phosphates.
NADPH supports reductive biosynthesis and regeneration of reduced glutathione. NADH more commonly supplies electrons for respiratory ATP production; the pools are functionally distinct.
Ribose-5-phosphate supplies nucleotide synthesis. Depending on cellular needs, nonoxidative reactions can connect pentoses with glycolytic intermediates.
Red blood cells rely on NADPH-dependent antioxidant defense. A pathway defect can increase oxidative vulnerability without implying that PPP directly produces ATP.
